name: Constantinople
span: c. 657 BCE – present (Constantinople from 330; internationally Istanbul since 1930)
info: A city on the Bosphorus in south-eastern Europe, settled by Greek colonists as Byzantium around 657 BCE, refounded by Constantine as Constantinople, capital of the Roman, Byzantine and Ottoman empires, and now Istanbul.

facts.founded: Settled by Greek colonists from Megara around 657 BCE as Byzantium, according to one source (another gives 667 or 685 BCE); the legend names a king Byzas; refounded by Constantine I in 324 and consecrated on 11 May 330
facts.where: A peninsula at the south-eastern tip of Thrace between the Golden Horn and the Sea of Marmara, on the European shore of the Bosphorus, in present-day Turkey
facts.known: The land walls of Theodosius II; Hagia Sophia; the Hippodrome and the Nika riots; capital of the Roman, Byzantine and Ottoman empires; the sack of 1204; the Ottoman conquest of 1453; the seat of the Ecumenical Patriarch
facts.today: It is the core of Istanbul, the largest city of Turkey, which has not been the capital since 1923.

t: The city was a Greek colony called Byzantium for nearly a thousand years before Constantine refounded it as a new capital in 330, and it was named Constantinople in his honour.
It was the capital of the Roman Empire in the east and then of the Byzantine Empire until the Ottoman conquest of 29 May 1453, and of the Ottoman Empire until the sultanate was abolished in 1922.
Its triple land walls kept out attackers for nearly nine hundred years, yet the city fell to a Christian army in 1204 and to an Ottoman army in 1453.
dyk: The name Istanbul comes from the Greek phrase eis tin Polin, 'to the city', which local people had long used; Turkey began to urge other countries to use it after 1930.
ev: Greek colonists from Megara settle Byzantium, according to one of the two sources
Septimius Severus razes Byzantium for backing Pescennius Niger, then rebuilds it and briefly renames it Augusta Antonina
Constantine consecrates the refounded city as the new capital of the Roman Empire, first called Nova Roma
Theodosius II builds the triple land walls, finished in 414
The Nika riots burn Hagia Sophia; Justinian's new church is dedicated in 537
The Fourth Crusade takes and plunders the city, and the Latin Empire holds it until 1261
Mehmed II takes Constantinople after a siege that began on 6 April
Turkey's government urges other countries to use the name Istanbul

sections.origins:
Byzantium stood on a peninsula at the south-eastern tip of Thrace, between the Golden Horn and the Sea of Marmara, across the Bosphorus from the town of Chalcedon. The site lay on the land route from Europe to Asia and on the sea route from the Black Sea to the Mediterranean, and the Golden Horn gave it a spacious harbour. People lived in the area from the Neolithic: a settlement dated to 6700 BCE was found in 2008 during work on the Yenikapı station and the Marmaray tunnel, and on the Asian side the Fikirtepe mound has artefacts from 5500 to 3500 BCE.

The city was founded around 657 BCE, according to one account, by colonists from the Greek city of Megara. Another account gives 667 BCE for Byzantion and 685 BCE for the settlement at Chalcedon, and the two do not agree. Greek legend names a king Byzas as the colonists' leader and as the founder who gave the city its name. Hesychius of Miletus reported that some claimed Megarians sailed there under Byzas and invented the story that his name was attached to the city, and he gave other versions as well. The name is also thought to be Thracian, perhaps from a personal name Byzas. Pliny the Elder named an earlier settlement, Lygos, possibly Thracian, whose few surviving walls lie near Seraglio Point.
sections.growth:
Byzantium was never a major city-state like Athens, Corinth or Sparta, but it had steady growth as a trading city. In 324 Constantine I refounded it on the site of the old town, at first as Nova Roma, and it was consecrated on 11 May 330. He divided it into 14 regions, as Rome was divided. The building was done in great haste, and columns, marbles, doors and tiles were taken from temples across the empire. On 18 May 332 he announced free distributions of food, said at the time to have been 80,000 rations a day from 117 points. The Hippodrome seated over 80,000 people, and the Mese, a colonnaded street, ran from the Augustaion to the Golden Gate.

In 413 and 414 Theodosius II built the 18-metre triple land walls, and on 27 February 425 he founded a university. Under Justinian I the population reached about 500,000, though some scholars suggest it could have been higher. Hagia Sophia was dedicated on 26 December 537 and is said to have cost 20,000 pounds of gold. From the mid-5th century to the early 13th century the city was the largest and wealthiest in Europe, and in the 9th and 10th centuries its population was between 500,000 and 800,000. The Ottoman city grew from about 80,000 at the death of Mehmed II to 300,000 by the 18th century.
sections.rulers:
Byzantium was annexed by Darius I in 512 BCE, because the Bosphorus was narrowest there and suited a pontoon bridge. A Greek army under the Spartan Pausanias took it in 478 BCE, and it was subordinate to Athens and, after 411 BCE, to Sparta. A treaty with Rome of about 150 BCE let it enter Roman rule unharmed. After it sided with Pescennius Niger, Septimius Severus besieged and razed it in 196, then rebuilt it, and for a time it was called Augusta Antonina. The name was soon dropped.

Constantine proclaimed the city the capital in 330, and it became the sole capital of the Roman Empire once the west was lost in the 5th century. The Komnenian dynasty ruled from 1081 to 1185. After the sack of 1204 the Latin Empire held the city, with Baldwin of Flanders chosen as its first emperor, until Michael VIII Palaiologos recaptured it in 1261. The Palaiologan emperors moved their residence to the Blachernae palace. By the early 15th century the empire was reduced to Constantinople and its surroundings and the despotate of Morea.

Mehmed II made it the fourth and final Ottoman capital in 1453, and it remained one until the sultanate was abolished in 1922. The Republic of Turkey was proclaimed on 29 October 1923 and the capital moved to Ankara.
sections.life:
The city's by-names included Basileuousa, the Queen of Cities, and in everyday Greek it was simply the City. Under the Byzantines it was a Greek-speaking city and the seat of the Ecumenical Patriarch. The Book of the Eparch, of the 10th century, shows tradesmen organised in guilds supervised by the Eparch, who regulated production, prices, imports and exports; each guild had a monopoly and no one could belong to two. Chariot racing in the Hippodrome gave the Blues and the Greens a political voice, and the people there acclaimed new emperors and criticised ministers. Procopius claimed that more than 500 prostitutes worked along the Mese, and Ibn Battuta, who travelled there in 1325, wrote that most of the artisans and sellers in the bazaars were women.

In the 12th century Venetians had trading quarters on the north side of the Golden Horn. Toward the end of Manuel I Komnenos's reign about 60,000 to 80,000 foreigners lived in a city of about 400,000, and in 1171 there was a Jewish community of 2,500. In 980 Basil II received 6,000 Varangian warriors from Prince Vladimir of Kiev as a bodyguard.

After 1453 Mehmed II brought Muslims, Christians and Jews in by force and by invitation. The census of 1477 counted 9,486 houses of Muslims, 3,743 of Greeks and 1,647 of Jews. The Grand Bazaar dates from 1455 and Topkapı Palace from 1459. Mehmed re-established the Orthodox patriarchate, and the architect Sinan designed many mosques under Suleiman I.
sections.crises:
The Nika riots of 532 began in the Hippodrome among the Blues and Greens. According to Procopius over 30,000 people were involved. The fires set by the mobs burned the Theodosian church of Hagia Sophia, which Justinian replaced. The Plague of Justinian struck in 541 and 542 and killed, by one estimate, 20 to 40 per cent of the inhabitants, though revisionist historians suggest fewer. The Arab Umayyads besieged the city in 674 to 678 and 717 to 718, and the walls held while Greek fire destroyed their fleets.

In 1203 the Fourth Crusade was diverted against Constantinople and breached the sea walls on 27 July. After a second rising in February 1204 an attack failed on 6 April and another from the Golden Horn succeeded on 12 April, and the city was given over to pillage for three days. Steven Runciman called the sack unparalleled in history and described murder, rape and the destruction of churches and libraries. Alice-Mary Talbot cites an estimated population of 400,000, about a third of whom were homeless afterwards.

When Michael VIII took the city in 1261 it had 35,000 people, and the Black Death reached it in 1347. In 1453 it held about 50,000 by one count, and 30,000 to 36,000 by another. George Sphrantzes counted 4,773 Greek defenders, 200 foreigners and about 3,000 volunteers for a perimeter of twelve miles. Mehmed II besieged the city from 6 April, using a cannon cast by the Hungarian Urban, and it fell on 29 May 1453. Soldiers were given three days to plunder, and the number of people taken captive is given as about 33,000 or 45,000.
sections.legacy:
Hagia Sophia was made a mosque after the conquest of 1453, and the Church of the Holy Apostles was pulled down to make room for the tomb of Mehmed II. Byzantine gold coinage, the solidus, became the bezant used across the Middle Ages. When the city fell, thousands of Greek and Latin manuscripts were taken by refugees to Italy, where they helped stimulate the Renaissance. The city's bishop, who came to be called the Ecumenical Patriarch, made it a centre of Christianity alongside Rome, and this contributed to the differences that led to the Great Schism of 1054. In Islamic belief the conquest of Constantinople is one of the signs of the end time.

The name changed slowly. Istanbul comes from the Greek eis tin Polin and is first attested in Armenian and Arabic from the 10th century. The Ottomans used it and also Kostantiniyye, and Western languages mostly kept Constantinople until the early 20th century. After the Latin alphabet was adopted in 1928 Turkey urged other countries to use Istanbul, and the United States State Department did so from May 1930. The population fell from an estimated 1,125,000 in 1914 to about 500,000 in 1924, and many Greeks and Armenians left, a departure hastened by the Istanbul pogrom of September 1955. By 2000 the metropolitan population exceeded 10 million.

summary: Founded as the Greek colony of Byzantium around 657 BCE, the city was refounded by Constantine in 330 and was capital of the Roman, Byzantine and Ottoman empires. Besieged many times, it was sacked in 1204 and taken by the Ottomans in 1453, and is now Istanbul.
notes: Founding date: the Constantinople article says around 657 BCE; the History of Istanbul article says 660 BC in its lede and 667 BC (Byzantion) and 685 BC (Chalcedon) in its text. I used 657 BCE, hedged, and said the accounts differ.
The History of Istanbul says Hagia Sophia was ordered sacked by Mehmed on entering; the Constantinople article says it was avoided in the pillage by strict orders. I left the point out.
Captives in 1453: 33,000 (Constantinople article) and 45,000 (the same article, a later section); both given. Population in 1453: about 50,000 against 30,000 to 36,000 (Tedaldi); given as two counts.
The History article says the empire split officially in 395 on Theodosius I's death; the Constantinople article says the city became sole capital in the 5th century. I used only the latter.
The sea-wall breach on 27 July is in the Constantinople article under the 1203 diversion; the year 1203 is implied by 'diverted in 1203'.

Constantine XI's death in the fighting is in the History article only; I left it out, along with its odd siege details (a 48-day fight, a mobile tower) that conflict with the 53-day figure and the 6 April start.
The census of 1477 also lists 267 households of Christians from Crimea and 31 of 'Gypsies'; left out for space.
The 'span' key was requested. Istanbul was used in the Ottoman period as well; the span says 'internationally since 1930' to match the article.
The 'more than 16 million' of the Constantinople lede has no year and was left out. The 1955 pogrom is kept; 20th and 21st century attacks, protests and politics are left out.

Wanted but not found: the number killed in 1203-1204 or in 1453; the 1453 fate of the Genoese and Venetians; Ottoman population in the 16th century is only 'close to 700,000' in the History lede, which I did not use.
